title: The Convent on the Pincian: Pforr, the Lukasbund, and a Middle Ages Painted in Rome
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the birth in the old town
stops.date_confidence: attested; both Wikipedia editions and Wikidata Q705163 give 5 April 1788
stops.campa: On the fifth of April 1788 a son is born in Frankfurt am Main to Johann Georg Pforr, painter of horses and animals, and to Johanna Christiane Pforr, born Tischbein. The Tischbeins have supplied German painting with practitioners for three generations; the boy arrives inside the trade on his mother's side and inside the workshop on his father's. The sources name the city and not the house, so this coordinate marks the old town and not a doorway. They christen him Franz. He dies at twenty-four, and every picture he makes is finished before then.
suggested_refs: Frankfurt parish registers for April 1788, not consulted in this research

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the father's studio
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source dates the beginning of the instruction, only that the father taught him first
stops.campa: In his father's studio the boy learns to draw before he learns anything else. Johann Georg Pforr paints horses, cattle, market scenes, animals set in landscape, and his son copies them: the working stock of a Frankfurt painter who makes what a Frankfurt burgher will hang. English Wikipedia says only that Pforr received his earliest training from his father. The studio gives him the hand. It does not give him a subject, and the German Middle Ages, which he will spend his short life on, appear nowhere in his father's inventory.
suggested_refs: Surviving animal pieces by Johann Georg Pforr in Frankfurt collections

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the death of Johann Georg Pforr
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by English Wikipedia; no month or day located, so the date defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: Johann Georg Pforr dies in 1798, aged fifty-three. The English article gives the year and no day; the German article does not separate the father's death from the mother's at all, folding both into one sentence about a boy orphaned by twelve. The studio closes on a ten-year-old who has had his first and only teacher for as long as he has been able to hold a pencil. Frankfurt keeps the father's canvases of horses. The son will paint horses too, in armor, ridden by kings out of chronicles, in a city eight hundred miles south of here.
suggested_refs: Johann Georg Pforr (1745-1798), animal painter of Frankfurt

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, orphaned by twelve
stops.date_confidence: compressed by the source: German Wikipedia gives only 'both parents lost by about age twelve', with no separate date for the mother; the year 1800 is that compression, not a document
stops.campa: By about his twelfth year both parents are gone. German Wikipedia states it as a single milestone and supplies no cause and no dates for either death; the English article dates the father to 1798 and leaves the mother's year unstated. The record for Johanna Christiane Pforr, born Tischbein, closes without a sentence of its own. What survives is the arithmetic. A boy of twelve is left in a house of painters with no painter standing in it, and the Tischbein side of the family decides what becomes of him.
suggested_refs: Frankfurt death registers for Johanna Christiane Pforr, geb. Tischbein, not located

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the brother dies
stops.date_confidence: relative only: German Wikipedia says the brother died a year after the parents, which places it around 1801 without naming a year
stops.campa: About a year after the parents, the only brother dies. German Wikipedia carries the sequence and nothing else: not the brother's name, not his age, not the place. Frankfurt is used for this pin because Frankfurt is where the household was; Kassel, where Pforr goes next, is equally possible and equally undocumented, and no source consulted names either. Franz Pforr is the last of his house. He is thirteen or thereabouts, and it is his mother's family, not his father's, that comes for him.
suggested_refs: The Pforr household of Frankfurt, dispersed between 1798 and 1801

stops.name: Kassel, taken into the Tischbein house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: 'Ab 1801 foerderte er die Ausbildung von Franz Pforr ... in Kassel'
stops.campa: Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Younger, born at Haina in 1742, inspector of the Kassel picture gallery since 1775, is the brother of the boy's mother. From 1801 he takes his sister's son into his household and directs his training. The German article on the uncle says he supported and promoted that training; no source consulted asserts a formal guardianship, and the difference is left standing here rather than smoothed away. Kassel is a residence city with a princely collection and a working academy, and the orphan enters it as a relative of the man who keeps the pictures.
suggested_refs: Johann Heinrich Tischbein der Juengere (1742-1808), inspector of the Kassel Gemaeldegalerie

stops.name: Kassel, the gallery he is presumed to study in
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the uncle's post; no document places Pforr in the gallery rooms
stops.campa: The uncle's office is the inspectorship of the landgraves' collection, and the nephew lives in his household for four years. That Pforr studied among those old masters follows from the post and from nothing else; no source consulted names him in those rooms, and the inference is marked as one. The walls carry Dutch, Flemish and Italian painting, the ordinary academic diet. What Pforr will later want hangs nowhere in it: German panels older than Raphael, made by men who believed the things they painted.
suggested_refs: The Hessian landgraves' picture gallery at Kassel, under Tischbein's inspectorship 1775-1808

stops.name: Kassel, the Tischbein mechanism
stops.date_confidence: framing stop, placed at the end of the Kassel years; carries no dated event of its own
stops.campa: Kassel is the hinge. On one side stands a Frankfurt animal painter's workshop; on the other stand the Vienna Academy and a Roman convent. The Tischbeins are the mechanism between them, a Hessian painting dynasty with men inside the academies and the galleries. Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein, of the same house, lodged with Goethe on the Via del Corso in 1786 and painted him lying in the Campagna. A quarter century before Pforr reaches Rome, a Tischbein has made the journey and taken the address.
suggested_refs: The Tischbein painting dynasty of Hesse, from Johann Heinrich the Elder to Wilhelm of the Italienische Reise

segments.name: Vienna: The Academy and the Bond

stops.name: Vienna, admitted under Fueger
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1805; no month located, so the date defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: In 1805 he is admitted to the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, into the school of Heinrich Friedrich Fueger, director and portraitist, the leading Viennese exponent of a classicism drawn from antique statuary and French example. Pforr is seventeen. Five years later he writes his guardian Sarasin in Frankfurt a full account of these student years, and it opens by admitting what he brought with him. The Academy's premises for 1805 are not confirmed in the sources consulted; this pin inherits the St. Anna courtyard coordinate already fixed in Overbeck's file.
stops.quote: I came here with a great longing to learn something, but equipped only with superficial knowledge.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, 'Geschichte des Studiums in Wien', letter to his guardian Johann Jakob Sarasin, 1810, in Margaret Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 1886), vol. I, p. 77; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Heinrich Friedrich Fueger (1751-1818), director of the Vienna Academy
Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, archive.org/details/friedrichoverbec01howi
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 77

stops.name: Vienna, Overbeck arrives
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source dates the meeting; it is placed inside the Academy years 1805-1809
stops.campa: A merchant's son from Luebeck enters the same school. Friedrich Overbeck is a year younger, better dressed, better read, and visibly not made of the material the Academy grinds down. Pforr notices him at once and writes it down four years later for Sarasin, in the plain sequence of a man who has decided to tell the whole thing. No source consulted fixes the year they meet. Three years later the two of them found the Lukasbund together, and the year after that they leave for Rome and do not come back.
stops.quote: During this endeavor Overbeck came here, a young man from a good house and an excellent family, who stood out powerfully against the others. I soon became acquainted with him and found myself especially drawn to him.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 78; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, pp. 77-88, printing Pforr's Vienna letter entire
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 78

stops.name: Vienna, the self-portrait
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikimedia Commons dates a Pforr self-portrait to 1807; a date of 1810 circulates without located evidence, and the Staedel lists two self-portraits without settling the question
stops.campa: He paints himself. The date is the problem: Commons carries 1807, which sets the picture in Vienna, while 1810 also circulates and would set it in Rome, and the Staedel holds two self-portraits by his hand without adjudicating between them. The contradiction is recorded and not resolved. What the earlier date would show is a face still inside the Academy, a student of nineteen in a city where his teacher paints emperors, looking out of a panel he made in order to practice looking.
suggested_refs: Self-portraits of Franz Pforr in the Staedel Museum, Frankfurt

stops.name: Vienna, the epoch he would rather pass over
stops.date_confidence: undated by the source: Pforr's 1810 letter narrates the episode in sequence without giving a year; placed between the meeting and the reconciliation
stops.campa: Overbeck advances faster. Pforr, who cannot keep pace, feels the friendship turn in his hands, and every praise spoken of the other in his hearing takes something out of it. He tells Sarasin that he comes now to a passage he would gladly pass over in silence for his own honor, and that passing over it would take him too far from the truth. The confession sits in the middle of a letter written to justify his studies. The document that founds the Nazarene friendship is the document that records it dying first.
stops.quote: This young man's progress hurt me in my soul, since I could not keep pace with him; I envied him, and my affection vanished more and more with every word of praise I heard about him, and our friendship died almost as it began.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 79; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, p. 79, the envy passage
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 79

stops.name: Vienna, the confession and the terms
stops.date_confidence: undated by the source: the reconciliation is narrated in the 1810 letter without a year; placed in the second Academy year of the friendship
stops.campa: He goes to Overbeck and says it outright: the fault, the request for pardon, the request for the friendship back. Overbeck answers, deeply moved, that a closer bond has long been his own most ardent wish. They then set terms, and the terms are strange ones for two students: praise given by an outsider to either of them is to strike both exactly as blame would. The friendship is rebuilt as a discipline rather than an affection, and the Lukasbund, a year off, will be built on the same principle enlarged to six men.
stops.quote: Openness is always best in such matters; I confessed my fault, asked forgiveness and his friendship, and he assured me, deeply moved, that it had long been his most ardent wish to see a closer bond between us.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, pp. 80-81; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, pp. 80-81, the reconciliation and its conditions
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, pp. 80-81

stops.name: Vienna, what Overbeck teaches him
stops.date_confidence: undated by the source; placed with the other reconciliation passages of the 1810 letter
stops.campa: Pforr reaches for Lessing to say what has happened to him and finds Lessing insufficient. The thinking artist is worth twice as much again, runs the borrowed maxim; the feeling artist surpasses even him, and Pforr credits Overbeck with the demonstration. The correction carries the program of the coming brotherhood: not that thought is unnecessary, but that it ranks below conviction. Fueger's Academy teaches the first and has no way of examining the second. Pforr sets the maxim down as something he was shown rather than something he reasoned out.
stops.quote: Lessing says: 'The thinking artist is worth twice as much again'; but that the feeling artist far surpasses even him, Overbeck showed me.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 81; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, p. 81
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 81

stops.name: Vienna, the Entry of Rudolf begun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: the Staedel catalogue and Wikimedia Commons both date the painting 1808-1810; the Web Gallery of Art's looser 1809-10 is the outlier
stops.campa: He begins the large canvas: the entry of King Rudolf of Habsburg into Basel in 1273, a medieval city gate, a crowd, banners, a horse painted by a horse painter's son. He has never seen Basel and will never see it. The Staedel dates the work 1808 to 1810, which means it is started in Vienna, rolled up, carried over the Alps, and finished in Rome; the frequent claim that it was painted entirely at Sant'Isidoro cannot stand against the museum's own dates. Ninety by a hundred and nineteen centimeters, oil on canvas.
suggested_refs: Franz Pforr, Der Einzug Kaiser Rudolfs von Habsburg in Basel 1273, Staedel Museum, Frankfurt

stops.name: Vienna, drawing away from the Academy
stops.date_confidence: undated within the 1810 letter; placed in the months before the July 1809 founding, which the letter treats as its outcome
stops.campa: The circle meets on its own time and works from its own models: German and early Italian panels, outline over modelling, honesty of contour over the polished machine of the life class. Pforr sees exactly what the practice costs them and writes it down without apology, in the flat accounting voice he uses for everything. Each step away from Fueger is a step toward the old painters, and the progress made in company is worth the discipline lost. A twenty-one-year-old states the argument of the Nazarene movement in a letter home, before the movement exists.
stops.quote: We found, indeed, that the further we went on in this way, the more we distanced ourselves from the principles of the Academy; but we found, on the other hand, that we drew ever closer to the manner of the old painters, and the progress our fellowship made was considerable.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 86; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, p. 86; the passage is also quoted, compressed, on German Wikipedia
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 86

stops.name: Vienna, the hands joined
stops.date_confidence: attested by Pforr's own letter, which dates the founding supper to 10 July 1809, one year after the circle began meeting
stops.campa: At a supper on the tenth of July 1809, a year to the day after the circle first began meeting regularly, they give each other their hands and a bond is concluded. Pforr's sentence for it is six words long and contains a hope rather than a claim. They name themselves for Saint Luke, patron of painters and, by tradition, the first man to paint the Virgin from life: the Lukasbund, the Brotherhood of Saint Luke. Overbeck's own account fixes the same founding at this same courtyard, and the two agree down to the place.
stops.quote: We joined hands, and a bond was sealed which, we hoped, would stand firm.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, describing the supper of 10 July 1809, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 86; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: The Lukasbund's founding supper, 10 July 1809, Vienna
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 86

stops.name: Vienna, the six who sign
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1809; the German articles on the Lukasbund and on Nazarene art give the year and the roster, not a day
stops.campa: Six names, and the roster has been miscopied often enough to be worth setting down: Franz Pforr, Friedrich Overbeck, Joseph Sutter, Josef Wintergerst, Johann Konrad Hottinger, Ludwig Vogel. Johann Nepomuk Hoefel, who appears in some lists, is a Vienna associate of the circle and not one of the six in the German articles on the Lukasbund and on Nazarene art. Two Swiss, one Swabian, one Luebecker, one Frankfurter, one Viennese: a brotherhood assembled out of a dissolving empire, taking Duerer and Perugino against the late manner of Raphael.
suggested_refs: de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lukasbund, founding roster of 1809

stops.name: Vienna, not readmitted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1809; no month located, so the date defaults within that year
stops.campa: The Academy must cut its student numbers in 1809, and the Lukasbrueder are simply not taken back. The mechanism is administrative, not doctrinal, whatever the movement's later legend prefers; German Wikipedia's article on the Lukasbund records a non-renewal and no expulsion for heresy against the antique. Overbeck does not leave with them: he breaks off his own Vienna studies in 1810, out of dissatisfaction with the classicism taught there. The distinction is small and the sources keep it, so this file keeps it too.
suggested_refs: de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lukasbund on the 1809 reduction of student numbers

stops.name: Vienna, the letter to Sarasin closes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1810 by Howitt, who dates the report to that year; no month given
stops.campa: He finishes the account for his guardian and signs it Franz Pforr. The last paragraph is not a defense of his studies but a declaration of subject matter: the Middle Ages, where he holds that the dignity of man still shows itself at full strength, in council chamber and marketplace and household as much as on the battlefield. He notes that the age is beautiful and that painters have barely used it. Within months he will be over the Alps looking for pictures made inside that age by men who had no idea they were living in it.
stops.quote: My inclination draws me to the age of the Middle Ages, where the dignity of man still shows itself in full force. On the battlefield as in the council chamber, in the marketplace as in the domestic circle, it expresses itself clearly and distinctly; the spirit of that age is so beautiful, and so little used by artists.
stops.quote_source: Franz Pforr, letter to Sarasin, Vienna, 1810, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 87; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, pp. 87-88, the close and signature of Pforr's report
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, pp. 87-88

stops.name: Brenner Pass, the crossing not documented
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year of the journey is attested, the month is not, and no source consulted names the route, the stopping towns, or the mode of travel
stops.campa: They go south in 1810. No source consulted records how. The Brenner corridor is the road German travelers take to Italy in this period, and this pin sits at the pass itself as a reconstruction and nothing more; the itinerary is a gap in the record, stated as a gap. What is certain is the freight: an unfinished canvas of a thirteenth-century king entering Basel, rolled and carried over the Alps by a painter of twenty-two who is leaving the German-speaking world for good.
suggested_refs: The Brenner route between Vienna and Italy, c. 1810; no Pforr itinerary located

stops.name: Rome, the quarter below the Trinita dei Monti
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1810 in Overbeck's atlas file; the day is not given
stops.campa: Pforr arrives in Rome with Overbeck, Ludwig Vogel and Johann Konrad Hottinger and lodges in the foreigners' quarter below the Trinita dei Monti, above the Piazza di Spagna. It is the same patch of the city where Wilhelm Tischbein lodged on a Kassel stipend three decades earlier; the coordinate is byte-identical across the two files and is inherited here. They have not come for the Rome of the Forum. They have come for the Rome underneath it, the churches and cloisters of a Christian city that the antique one is standing on.
suggested_refs: The German artists' colony around the Piazza di Spagna and the Trinita dei Monti

stops.name: Rome, Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1810; the month follows the pin already canonical in Overbeck's file
stops.campa: Four of the brotherhood take rooms in the half-abandoned Franciscan convent of Sant'Isidoro on the slope of the Pincian, and live there under a rule of their own making: cells, shared meals, communal criticism of each other's work, the medieval workshop reconstructed by young men who have read about it. The Napoleonic suppressions have emptied the house and left the cells available to whoever wants them. The street outside will later be renamed Via degli Artisti for the people now moving in.
suggested_refs: Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case, Rome, occupied by the Nazarenes 1810-1820

stops.name: Rome, the name the city gives them
stops.date_confidence: undated: the nickname's origin is not fixed to a moment by any source consulted; placed early in the convent years
stops.campa: They wear their hair long and parted in the middle and dress plainly, in what they take to be the manner of the old German masters, and Rome laughs at them for it. One theory, the one German Wikipedia's article on Nazarene art carries, derives the nickname from the seventeenth-century Roman hairstyle alla nazarena and reports it as mockery. The article presents this as a theory and not as a settled etymology, and the hedge is kept here. Nazarener: the insult becomes the name of the movement and outlives everyone who was mocked.
suggested_refs: de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazarener_(Kunst) on the hairstyle alla nazarena

stops.name: Rome, Overbeck paints Pforr
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1810; no month located
stops.campa: Overbeck makes the Portrait of the Painter Franz Pforr in 1810: his friend seated in a Gothic window frame, a medieval town behind him, a woman knitting in the room beyond, a cat, a lily, a vine. It is a portrait built as an altarpiece and it puts Pforr inside the century he says he belongs to. Most of what the world can see of Pforr's face comes from the hand of the man he once envied for painting better. He has under two years left, and neither of them knows it in October.
suggested_refs: Friedrich Overbeck, Bildnis des Malers Franz Pforr, 1810

stops.name: Rome, Raphael, Fra Angelico and Michelangelo over the city
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1810 by the Web Gallery of Art; no month located
stops.campa: He draws the three of them in pencil, hovering above Rome: Raphael, Fra Angelico, Michelangelo, the tribunal the Lukasbund has appointed over itself. Fra Angelico is the surprise in that company and the reason it counts as a statement: a Dominican who painted on his knees, set level with the two men the academies teach as the summit of art. The drawing is a program with faces. Pforr has been in the city a few months and has already decided which of its dead he intends to answer to.
suggested_refs: Franz Pforr, Raphael, Fra Angelico and Michelangelo over Rome, pencil, 1810

stops.name: Rome, the Entry of Rudolf finished
stops.date_confidence: the Staedel dates the picture 1808-1810; the month of completion is not recorded, and December is the end of the attested span rather than a documented date
stops.campa: The Basel canvas is finished in Rome, two years after it was begun in Vienna. King Rudolf of Habsburg rides in through the gate in 1273; the burghers line the street; the composition is flat and bright, in the manner of the panels Pforr prefers to his own century. The picture hangs today in the Staedel in Frankfurt, oil on canvas, ninety and a half by a hundred and nineteen centimeters, on permanent loan from the Historisches Museum Frankfurt since 1922. The Staedel shows it. The Staedel does not own it.
suggested_refs: Der Einzug Kaiser Rudolfs von Habsburg in Basel 1273, Staedel Museum, on loan from Historisches Museum Frankfurt since 1922

stops.name: Rome, the house Goethe kept
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1811 in Overbeck's atlas file; no day given
stops.campa: The brotherhood takes an apartment on the Via del Corso, the house Goethe once called home. It is number 18, the lodging Goethe shared with Wilhelm Tischbein in 1786 and 1787 and called his second birth. Twenty-five years later the Nazarenes are sleeping in it, hunting for exactly the opposite of what Goethe found there: not the antique, but the age the antique's admirers call dark. The same rooms now hold a third generation of Germans abroad, still chasing what an earlier one came to Rome to leave behind.
suggested_refs: Casa di Goethe, Via del Corso 18, Rome

stops.name: Vatican, the Stanze of Raphael
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the group's study of the Vatican frescoes is documented as a practice, but no source consulted places Pforr individually in these rooms on any date
stops.campa: The Nazarenes work in the Stanze, copying Raphael before the Raphael they reject, the early frescoes rather than the late machines. The distinction is the axis of the movement: Perugino's pupil against the master of the Farnesina. Whether Pforr himself stood in these rooms is not separately attested in the sources consulted, and the pin marks a group practice rather than a documented visit. Michelangelo's ceiling is a few minutes' walk from here, and the same qualification covers it.
suggested_refs: The Stanze di Raffaello, Vatican Palace

stops.name: Rome, Sulamith and Maria
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1810-1811 by the Web Gallery of Art; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: A panel thirty-four by thirty-two centimeters, two women set side by side: Sulamith dark and Italian, Maria fair and German, the sensuous ideal and the chaste one, each in her own landscape and her own architecture. It is a marriage allegory and a friendship allegory at the same time, and German Wikipedia calls it archetypal for the Nazarene sensibility. The picture is now at the Museum Georg Schaefer in Schweinfurt, a private collection until it opened as a public museum in 2000, which is why older catalogues list it as privately held.
suggested_refs: Franz Pforr, Sulamith und Maria, 1810-11, Museum Georg Schaefer, Schweinfurt

stops.name: Rome, Saint George and the Dragon
stops.date_confidence: the Web Gallery of Art gives 'around 1811'; no month or firm year is recorded
stops.campa: Oil on wood, twenty-eight by twenty-one centimeters: the knight, the lance, the worm, the princess, the whole chivalric apparatus painted small and bright like a devotional panel from four centuries earlier. It is the Middle Ages of his letter to Sarasin, executed. The picture then disappears from view for over a century and is rediscovered only in 1923, by whom and out of where the German article does not say. The output of these Roman years is small enough that a single panel going missing is a measurable loss to it.
suggested_refs: Franz Pforr, Sankt Georg der Drachentoeter, c. 1811, Staedel Museum, Frankfurt

stops.name: Rome, the roster that never assembles
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1811 for the arrival of Cornelius and Schadow; no month located
stops.campa: Peter von Cornelius and Wilhelm von Schadow reach the Sant'Isidoro circle in 1811, and Philipp Veit not until 1815. These are the names the Nazarene movement is remembered by, the men who will carry it into the Casa Bartholdy frescoes and then into the directorships of half the German academies. Pforr, in the convent since 1810, is dead before the famous roster is ever in one room together. The movement he founds becomes an institution and he is not present for a single day of it.
suggested_refs: The second wave of the Nazarenes: Cornelius and Schadow (1811), Veit (1815)

stops.name: Rome, the Christmas table
stops.date_confidence: attested: Overbeck's diary heading gives Tuesday the 24th, Christmas Eve, under the running head 1811-1812; Howitt's own commentary calls this the surprise prepared by the sick Pforr, which fixes the year as 1811
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve Pforr surprises the brotherhood with a Bescherung. Overbeck's little Madonna is set on a lighted table dressed with foliage, and there is a present laid out for each of them; Overbeck's own is an antique bowl filled with oranges and grapes. He is already ill. Howitt, printing the diary seventy-five years later, calls this the surprise the sick Pforr prepared for his friends and nurses. He has under six months left, and he spends this evening arranging gifts for the men who will bury him.
stops.quote: In the evening Pforr gave us great joy with a gift-giving, with which he surprised us.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Overbeck, Roman diary, Tuesday 24 December 1811 (Christmas Eve), in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 223; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, p. 223, the Christmas Eve entry
sources: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck (1886), vol. I, p. 223

stops.name: Rome, an hour of talk in February
stops.date_confidence: attested: the diary heading reads Sunday, 16 February, within the section headed 1812, and a footnote fixing Ash Wednesday at 12 February confirms the 16th as a Sunday
stops.campa: On a Sunday in February Overbeck sits with him for an hour and writes it down that night. The tone is of something recovered rather than something ordinary: the old relationship, the conversations about art, the evenings when the two of them built the loveliest ideals between them. That is the register a man uses about a friend he is losing. The chapter of Howitt's biography in which the entry sits is headed Duestere Schatten, Gloomy Shadows, and covers the last illness from its beginning.
stops.quote: So I have at last, once again, spent an hour chatting with Pforr, which truly reminded me of our old relationship, of our sweet conversations about art, of the evenings when together we fashioned for ourselves the loveliest ideals.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Overbeck, Roman diary, Sunday 16 February 1812, in Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen (1886), vol. I, p. 225, chapter 'Duestere Schatten'; translation by the atlas
suggested_refs: Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck, vol. I, p. 225

stops.name: Rome, the illness advancing
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sources attest tuberculosis in his final Roman period without dating its stages; April is placed between the February diary entry and the move to Albano
stops.campa: The tuberculosis takes its course. Neither Wikipedia article details the progress of the disease, and no record of any physician, treatment or hospital in Rome was located in this research; the medical history is a gap and is stated as one. He is twenty-three. Around him the convent continues, Cornelius and Schadow at work, the frescoed decade ahead of them all, and the man who wrote the founding letter is being nursed by his brothers in a cell on the Pincian.
suggested_refs: Roman medical records for the German artists' colony, 1812; none located

stops.name: Albano Laziale, sent up into the hills
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sources place his death at Albano without dating the move; May is placed before the attested June death
stops.campa: He is moved out to Albano Laziale, in the Castelli Romani above the plain, where Romans and resident foreigners have gone for centuries to escape the summer fevers and breathe cleaner air. It is the standard prescription of the period and it does nothing for tuberculosis. The lake and the old Appian road are below; Rome is fifteen miles north. The date of the move is not recorded in the sources consulted, and the last painting he works on is not identified in them either.
suggested_refs: Albano Laziale and the Castelli Romani as a summer refuge from Roman fevers

stops.name: Albano Laziale, the death at twenty-four
stops.date_confidence: 16 June 1812 is given by German Wikipedia, by Wikidata Q705163, and by the body text of the English article; only the English infobox gives 12 June, and that outlier is recorded rather than treated as a genuine disagreement between sources
stops.campa: Franz Pforr dies at Albano Laziale on the sixteenth of June 1812, of tuberculosis, aged twenty-four years and two months. He has been in Italy twenty-three months. He leaves one completed history painting, two small panels, and drawings that German Wikipedia counts only as several hundred. The English infobox carries 12 June against the body text of its own article; German Wikipedia and Wikidata give the sixteenth, and the outlier is one uncorrected field rather than a second tradition.
suggested_refs: Albano Laziale death records for June 1812, not located in this research

stops.name: Albano Laziale, the grave nobody has found
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source consulted records the burial at all, and the date here is a placeholder two days after the attested death
stops.campa: He is buried at Albano. That is the whole of it. Repeated targeted searching of German and English Wikipedia, of Wikidata Q705163, and of the open web returned no church, no cemetery, no plaque and no tomb; the burial place of the founder of the Nazarene movement is not recorded in anything reachable from this desk. The coordinate marks the town and not a grave. The gap is stated as a gap, and the men in the convent who nursed him kept no record of it that has come down.
suggested_refs: Parish and cemetery records of Albano Laziale, 1812; not located

segments.name: Afterlife: The Picture He Does Not See

stops.name: Rome, Overbeck received into the Roman church
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1813 by German Wikipedia; no day located
stops.campa: Ten months after the death Overbeck converts to Catholicism, in April 1813. The German article on him credits the influence of the future cardinal Pietro Ostini and does not mention Pforr in connection with it. Biographers have nonetheless read the loss of his closest collaborator into the timing, and that reading is carried here as an interpretation without a located source rather than as a fact. The pin is the Rome coordinate already used across Overbeck's file, inherited here unchanged.
suggested_refs: Pietro Ostini (1775-1849), later cardinal, named in the German account of Overbeck's conversion

stops.name: Rome, Sant'Isidoro empties
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1820 as the end of the Nazarene occupation of the convent; no month given, and the wider movement's dispersal is a separate event dated 1830
stops.campa: The Nazarenes occupy the convent from 1810 to 1820, and then the common life ends: members marry, convert, take commissions across the city, move into the Palazzo Zuccari and the Casa Bartholdy a few hundred meters away. The circle spends a decade inside a five-hundred-meter radius of the Pincian slope. The movement's own dissolution comes later, by 1830, when all of them except Overbeck have gone back to Germany to teach. Two dispersals, eighteen years apart, are often reported as one.
suggested_refs: Casa Bartholdy frescoes, Palazzo Zuccari, Rome, 1816-1817

stops.name: Rome, Italia und Germania
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1811-1828 for the painting; 1828 is the completion year, the month is not recorded
stops.campa: Overbeck finishes the picture he has been at since 1811: two women seated hand in hand, one dark and Italian, one fair and German, against their two landscapes. German Wikipedia states that it goes back to Pforr's drawing Allegorie der Freundschaft, to his text, and to Sulamith und Maria. Ninety-four by a hundred and five centimeters, oil on canvas, now in the Neue Pinakothek in Munich. It takes seventeen years to paint and it answers a panel by a man who has been dead for sixteen of them. Pforr does not see it.
suggested_refs: Friedrich Overbeck, Italia und Germania, 1811-1828, Neue Pinakothek, Munich

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, the letters printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the publication year 1886
stops.campa: Margaret Howitt's life of Overbeck is published at Freiburg by Herder, and inside its first volume, at pages 77 to 88, stands the whole of Pforr's report to Sarasin on his studies in Vienna: the arrival with superficial knowledge, the envy, the confession, the pact, the ten days of July, the Middle Ages. It survives because Overbeck kept a copy of it. Almost everything quotable of Pforr's own words passes through a book about somebody else, written seventy-four years after Pforr wrote the sentences, and it has never been published in English.
suggested_refs: Margaret Howitt, Friedrich Overbeck: Sein Leben und Schaffen, ed. Franz Binder, 2 vols., Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 1886; scanned at archive.org/details/friedrichoverbec01howi

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Staedel takes the Basel picture
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1922 by the Staedel catalogue entry for the permanent loan; no month given
stops.campa: The Entry of King Rudolf of Habsburg into Basel comes to the Staedel in 1922, on permanent loan from the Historisches Museum Frankfurt am Main. A painter born in Frankfurt in 1788 has his largest surviving picture hung in Frankfurt a hundred and thirty-four years later, by an arrangement between two municipal institutions and not by any act of his own. The Staedel's collection database now documents seventy-six works by his hand, which is the one hard number the record supplies for an output usually described in adjectives.
suggested_refs: Staedel Museum, Frankfurt: 76 works by Franz Pforr, sammlung.staedelmuseum.de/en/person/pforr-franz

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Saint George resurfaces
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1923 by German Wikipedia; the circumstances and the finder are not recorded
stops.campa: The little Saint George panel is rediscovered in 1923, more than a century after it was painted and the year after the Basel canvas comes to the Staedel. German Wikipedia gives the year and nothing else: not where it had been, not who found it, not how it was identified. His papers meanwhile sit in two libraries, at the Universitaetsbibliothek Johann Christian Senckenberg in Frankfurt under the shelfmark Ms. Ff. F. Pforr, and at the city library of Luebeck, which is Overbeck's town and not his.
suggested_refs: Universitaetsbibliothek Johann Christian Senckenberg, Frankfurt, Ms. Ff. F. Pforr; Stadtbibliothek Luebeck
